analysis.one_liner: Lets bankruptcy judges cut mortgage balances to a home's current value for struggling owners.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors in October 2007, sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee, and never received a vote as the foreclosure crisis grew.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let people in Chapter 13 bankruptcy — the kind where you repay debts on a court-approved plan — ask a judge to reduce their home mortgage balance to what the house is actually worth, waive prepayment penalties, and freeze or undo adjustable-rate increases. It applied only to mortgages taken out before late September 2007, only to households below roughly 150% of their state's median income, and it expired after seven years. It also let people whose lender had already started foreclosure skip the pre-filing credit counseling requirement, and directed a study of how mortgage write-downs would affect the market that buys mortgages from lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners whose houses were worth less than they owed and who filed Chapter 13 bankruptcy would have been able to strip the unpaid balance down to the home's fair market value, keeping them in their homes instead of losing them to foreclosure [S2][S3]. The relief was limited to lower-income households and to loans made before September 26, 2007, and it would have ended after seven years [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bankruptcy judges could lower a mortgage's principal to the home's fair market value when the loan exceeded the house's worth, and waive prepayment penalties [S2][S3].
For adjustable-rate mortgages, courts could prohibit, delay, or void interest-rate adjustments, including ones made in the two years before filing [S2][S3].

A borrower whose lender had begun foreclosure could delay the credit counseling requirement that normally must be completed before filing bankruptcy, so a filing could happen fast enough to stop the foreclosure [S2][S3].
Courts could treat undisclosed interest and fees on a home mortgage as voidable transfers when a lender substantially failed to disclose material loan terms [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and the investors who hold mortgage debt would have absorbed the loss when judges wrote loan balances down to the home's current value, and lenders could no longer collect prepayment penalties or some rate increases from borrowers in bankruptcy [S2][S3]. If write-downs raised the perceived risk of mortgage lending, future borrowers could face higher rates or tighter credit [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage lenders and mortgage debt investors

drawbacks.text: The bill applied retroactively to loans made before September 26, 2007, changing the terms of existing contracts, and it directed a study of the impact on the secondary mortgage market — an acknowledgment that write-downs could make mortgage lending riskier and more expensive for future homebuyers [S2][S3].

Relief was narrow: only households below roughly 150% of state median income qualified, only pre-September 2007 loans were covered, and the whole provision sunset after seven years, so it was a one-time intervention rather than a lasting fix [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For homeowners facing foreclosure on houses worth less than their loans, the relief could mean keeping a home rather than losing it, and the income caps and sunset limited the scope of the change. The main cost falls on lenders and mortgage investors, though if write-downs raised borrowing costs, that cost would spread to future buyers. The bill was drafted narrowly and included a required study of the secondary-market effects, which suggests its sponsor recognized the tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Chabot introduced the bill on October 9, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On November 2, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without the House ever voting on the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors in mortgage debt were better off, since no judge ever wrote down a loan balance under this bill; homeowners in foreclosure got no relief from it.

for.name: Rep. Steve Chabot
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; after a subcommittee referral on November 2, 2007, no further action occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern appears in the record.

industries.note: Judges could have cut loan balances to home values, waived prepayment penalties, and voided rate increases on borrowers in bankruptcy, directly reducing what lenders collect. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the interests of homeowners facing foreclosure.

Investors holding mortgage debt would have absorbed write-downs, which is why the bill ordered a study of the effect on the secondary mortgage market. Avoiding write-downs preserved their returns at the cost of more foreclosures for borrowers.
